title: Content-faithful reading and writing of specific episodic memories

concept.text: The proposed innovation is the ability to recover the detailed content of a particular remembered episode from brain activity and to install specified episodic content without the corresponding experience. Readout would identify what happened—people, places, event order and sensory details—with fidelity to the subject’s recollection. Write-in would produce content that later reports and behavior express as a memory, rather than merely prompting a story or teaching a response. These are target capabilities; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate their achievement.

The accompanying scientific goal is a causal account connecting particular episodic content to molecular changes, synapses and distributed neural ensembles. Performing the operations would be a major advance, but an effective decoder or stimulation procedure would not by itself explain how the memory is stored. The reviewed intracranial study illustrates this distinction: predicting selected concepts during recall did not establish that the decoded signal represented an episode-specific memory trace, and the neural features responsible for decoding remained uncertain.

As an operational distinction, tagging cells during learning and later reactivating them would not alone meet this goal. Such an intervention need not reveal the episode’s detailed content or allow an experimenter to specify a new episode. Likewise, recognizing a person-related concept, reconstructing language meaning and decoding imagined speech are relevant components, but each requires additional evidence before it can count as content-faithful episodic readout.

significance.text: Conditional scientific significance: reliable reading and writing of specific episodic content would make memory information experimentally accessible at a new level. Researchers could compare what was encoded with what is later retrieved, perturb selected content and test causal explanations of storage, retrieval and consolidation. The reviewed intracranial preprint motivates content-selective interventions and studies recall across an overnight design, but it does not demonstrate the proposed write-in capability.

Treating an identified traumatic memory or restoring a particular lost memory are possible downstream applications, not automatic consequences. They would require evidence of therapeutic control, safety, durability and specificity. Restoring an original memory would also require access to its original content or surviving trace: installing a plausible replacement would not establish recovery of what actually happened. The preprint’s discussion of selectively enhancing or muting memory is a prospective application rather than evidence of established treatment.

Broader implications are conditional synthesis. Effects on identity, learning or legal evidence would depend on technical reliability, consent, provenance and institutions beyond the laboratory demonstration. Successful manipulation of selected episodes would not establish a complete account of autobiographical memory or explain persistence over decades. Feasibility remains uncertain, and neither limited decoding nor a future successful write-in experiment should be treated as unrestricted access to a person’s past.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unresolved capability is distinguishing and recovering a particular episode rather than detecting concepts that also occur in other experiences. The reviewed intracranial manuscript explicitly leaves open whether its signal reflects an episode-specific trace or semantic and contextual information. A stronger system would have to recover how people, places and details were bound into one event, including temporal order, while separating that event from similar memories.

Engineering synthesis: readout must generalize beyond the episodes used to train or tune the model and distinguish neural evidence from plausible completion by a language model. It must also separate remembered content from current perception, imagined narration and the act of reporting. Participant-specific intracranial concept prediction and imperfect noninvasive semantic reconstruction leave substantial gaps in access, generalization and detail fidelity. The supplied evidence does not establish the full field-wide extent of these gaps.

Proposed write-in barriers include determining which neural changes specify the intended content, delivering those changes with sufficient precision and integrating them into later natural retrieval. Evidence would need to distinguish an installed episode from conditioning, suggestion, transient stimulation effects or a learned reporting strategy. The supplied sources do not settle the present-day status of arbitrary episodic write-in, so these are requirements of the target capability rather than a verified claim that every relevant intervention remains absent.

Mechanistic synthesis: linking operations to storage requires content-specific causal tests across molecular, synaptic and circuit levels. A perturbation that prevents recall could instead impair perception, attention, reporting or retrieval generally. Identifying some necessary features would narrow the mechanism without proving sufficiency or completeness. Explaining long-term persistence would require additional longitudinal evidence; it cannot be inferred from short-term operational success.

current_state.text: The reviewed version of the bioRxiv study is dated October 1, 2026, although its DOI and original research notes refer to 2025. It reports participant-specific models trained on intracranial spike recordings during a single viewing of a television episode in patients undergoing epilepsy monitoring. The models predicted subsequent recall of eight selected concepts, chosen using screen time and recall frequency, with above-chance results and controls described in the reviewed text. This is constrained concept prediction using training from the same viewed episode, not generalization to wholly unseen episodes or detailed narrative reconstruction. The authors explicitly could not establish that the decoded signal was an episode-specific memory trace.

That manuscript identifies itself as a preprint not certified by peer review. This establishes the status of the reviewed version, not the absence of a journal publication elsewhere. The retained PDF text was truncated on page 32 and carried an extraction warning that some form content was skipped; the review nevertheless had the relevant methods, results and discussion passages. Two retained PDFs contained the same relevant text and do not constitute independent replication. The original 2025 version was not established by the supplied review, and the empty search record does not establish freshness beyond the dated material.

Tang, LeBel, Jain and Huth’s 2023 Nature Neuroscience study, reported in volume 26, pages 858–866, supports noninvasive reconstruction of aspects of meaning from perceived speech, imagined speech and silent videos. Subject cooperation was required both to train and to apply the decoder. The reviewed supplementary examples show overlap in meaning alongside changed wording and details, supporting semantic reconstruction rather than an exact transcript. This does not demonstrate detailed reconstruction of a specific remembered episode.

Access to the 2023 study was partial: the review used a subscription preview and supplementary text rather than the complete main article. The relevant supplement was truncated on page 23, and figure images and significance highlighting were not inspected. The research notes’ reported word-error range of 0.92–0.94 was not verified by the supplied review and is therefore not retained as an established measurement here. A PDF downloaded under this article’s source entry was actually an unrelated language-pretraining paper and supplies no neuroscience evidence.

Kunz and colleagues’ Cell study, reported in volume 188, pages 4658–4673.e17, dated August 21, 2025, concerns inner-speech decoding from motor cortex. The reviewed accepted manuscript supports real-time decoding of instructed imagined sentences and restricted findings involving uninstructed inner speech, including sequence-recall and counting tasks. It also states that complete, intelligible sentences during free-form thinking could not be accurately decoded. This is relevant progress in speech interfaces, but it does not establish episodic-memory readout or prove that speech and memory occupy wholly separate neural codes.

The Cell evidence available to the review was more extensive than the article summary described in the earlier research: an accepted-manuscript XML copy included substantial main text and methods. Its extraction was truncated in the references, and external supplements and figure images were not inspected. Those limits constrain interpretation of material beyond the reviewed text without negating the documented instructed-speech result or the stated free-form limitation.

The research notes attribute tagged-engram reactivation and induced retrieval to Josselyn and Tonegawa’s 2020 Science review. No saved text for that review was available in the supplied evidence review, so this packet cannot independently substantiate the earlier assertion that artificial retrieval is established. The attribution is preserved as unverified here, rather than treated as false. Even if substantiated, tagged-ensemble reactivation would still require additional demonstrations to meet the content-readout and specified-write-in definitions above.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed readout demonstration: for human episodes never used to build or tune the decoder, recover people, places, event sequence and sensory details that correspond to the subject’s report. Include unpredictable details and compare performance with models given only generic story priors, so plausible guessing cannot explain the result. Independent records of the original experience should help distinguish faithful decoding of a recollection from accuracy about the event itself, because a subject’s memory may contain errors. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Unseen episode readout matches recollection beyond generic story priors

completion_criteria.text: Proposed write-in demonstration: begin in animals with behavioral tests that distinguish specified episodic content from simple conditioning or a learned response, and consider consenting humans only later. The corresponding episode must not have been experienced. Retrieval should occur with natural cues, and independent provenance records should distinguish implanted content from lived events. A human report that implanted content feels remembered would be relevant, but should not substitute for controls on suggestion and reporting strategy. Reactivating a tagged fear ensemble alone would not qualify.
completion_criteria.label: Implanted unexperienced episodic content is retrieved through natural cues

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanistic demonstration: pair the operations with causal perturbations identifying molecular or synaptic features necessary for the particular episode. Control for general impairments in perception, reporting and retrieval, and test whether perturbations selectively affect the intended content while preserving comparison memories. Such results would connect the operation to storage mechanisms without establishing that all necessary features have been found or that a complete mechanism has been explained.
completion_criteria.label: Causal perturbations identify episode-specific storage features while preserving comparison memories

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: seek independent replication across participants, episodes and laboratories; report failures, detail errors, retention intervals, training demands and reliance on invasive access. Assess durability, unintended changes to other memories and the conditions under which subjects can decline or interrupt decoding. Finite demonstrations would establish breadth within tested conditions, not literal universality. No numerical success threshold is established by the supplied material.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication establishes breadth with practical limits and failures reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NEU-01, simultaneous spike-resolved recording from every neuron in a behaving mammalian brain, and NEU-02, whole-brain synaptic-resolution connectomics, concern comprehensive measurement. They could support searches for distributed memory representations and their structural substrates. NEU-04 asks what particular episodic content those measurements encode and how to manipulate it. Comprehensive recording or connectivity alone would not supply that interpretation, while a constrained memory demonstration might not require complete brain coverage.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-03 seeks a prospective theory predicting circuit computation from connectivity, while NEU-10 seeks a causal account of conscious content. Both intersect with interpreting neural representations. NEU-04 is specifically about retained episodic information and its retrieval or installation; circuit computation, conscious experience and remembered event content remain distinct explanatory targets.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-07, noninvasive cellular-resolution read and write through the intact human skull, and NEU-09, cell-type-specific molecular access throughout the intact adult human brain, could provide access for memory measurements and interventions. Access alone would not identify which signals or changes encode an episode. Conversely, an invasive, localized NEU-04 demonstration would not establish either broader access capability.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-06 concerns reconstruction of cognitive circuits after neuronal loss, and NEU-11 concerns reversible reopening of circuit-specific critical-period plasticity. Reconstructed neurons or altered plasticity could eventually help carry, restore or modify memories, but neither capability establishes preservation or installation of specified episodic content. Restoring circuit function and recovering an original lost episode require distinct evidence. These relationships follow from the supplied titles; detailed definitions were not provided.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-05, target-specific adult central nervous system axon regrowth, and NEU-08, a developmental code for building specified functional circuits, address structural repair or construction that could support future memory interventions. NEU-12 addresses replacing necessary sleep functions and could intersect with memory consolidation experiments. None is equivalent to demonstrating content-faithful episodic readout and write-in.

Editorial treatment: the research identifies a historical “complete engram” item with NEU-04. That historical definition was not supplied, so exact equivalence cannot be independently checked. The intended overlap is retained within NEU-04 without creating a second discovery or merging or deleting any supplied roster entry.

change_log.reason: The reviewed studies document limitations of particular approaches but do not establish the entire present-day status of episodic readout, write-in or storage mechanisms.

change_log.reason: These address the review’s scientific distinctions without presenting proposed benchmarks as consensus standards or finite tests as proof of universality.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to the supplied roster while retaining all entries and qualifying the historical complete-engram equivalence.
change_log.reason: Roster titles permit useful conceptual comparisons, but detailed definitions and the historical item were not supplied.

unresolved_issues: The supplied review does not establish the full contemporary status of detailed episodic readout, specified episodic write-in or the molecular-to-ensemble account of storage.
The original 2025 bioRxiv version, any subsequent journal publication and developments beyond the reviewed dated materials remain unverified; the supplied search record is empty.
The intracranial study leaves unresolved whether decoded signals represent an episode-specific memory trace rather than semantic or contextual information, and which neural features support decoding.
The Science engram-review attribution lacks a supplied artifact. The research also mentions a 2024 engram-linking review without a supplied reviewed source; it is not used as evidentiary support.
The research notes’ 0.92–0.94 word-error range remains unverified and requires its original measurement context before quantitative reuse.
Partial access, truncated extractions and uninspected figures or supplements limit conclusions beyond the passages described in the supplied review.
Detailed definitions of the other roster concepts and the historical complete-engram item remain unavailable; relationships beyond their titles cannot be confirmed.
The proposed demonstrations leave practical success thresholds, acceptable error rates, durability requirements and the sufficiency of animal behavioral evidence to be specified.
No substantive review recommendation was rejected; qualifications were retained where the packet could not resolve the underlying claim.

brief.title: Reading and creating detailed memories
possible: People could have the details of a remembered event read from brain activity, including who was there, what happened and in what order. Researchers could also install a specified event that someone later recalls as a memory, without having lived through it.
why: Researchers could compare what someone experienced with what they later remember, change selected details and test how the brain stores memories. This could open paths toward treating particular traumatic memories or restoring lost ones.

sources.showed: This review discusses triggering recall by reactivating brain cells tagged during learning.
sources.cited_for: It concerns experimental control over memory retrieval.
sources.not_established: Recovering detailed content and installing a specified new event would require further demonstrations.

sources.who: Yuanyi Ding, Soraya L. S. Dunn, John J. Sakon and colleagues
sources.showed: In a preprint, models trained on brain recordings during television viewing predicted selected concepts during later recall. Training was specific to each participant and the viewed episode.
sources.quote: individual participant models predict vocalization of specific concepts
sources.cited_for: Brain activity can predict selected people or places mentioned during recall.
sources.not_established: Whether the signals identify a particular remembered event remains unresolved.

sources.who: Jerry Tang, Amanda LeBel, Shailee Jain and Alexander G. Huth
sources.showed: Brain scans supported reconstruction of meaning from heard speech, imagined speech and silent videos. Participants had to cooperate during training and use.
sources.quote: Given novel brain recordings, this decoder generates intelligible word sequences that recover the meaning of perceived speech, imagined speech and even silent videos, demonstrating that a single decoder can be applied to a range of tasks.
sources.cited_for: Meaning can be reconstructed from brain recordings without implanted electrodes.
sources.not_established: Detailed reconstruction of a particular remembered event remains to be demonstrated.

sources.who: Erin M. Kunz, Benyamin Abramovich Krasa and colleagues
sources.showed: Researchers decoded instructed imagined sentences in real time from brain regions involved in movement. Unprompted inner speech results were limited to constrained tasks.
sources.quote: Using multi-unit recordings from four participants, we found that inner speech is robustly represented in motor cortex, and that imagined sentences can be decoded in real-time.
sources.cited_for: Imagined speech can be decoded during instructed tasks.
sources.not_established: Accurate decoding of complete sentences during free-form thinking and detailed memory readout remain beyond these results.

shown: Ding and colleagues predicted eight selected concepts during recall of a television episode using implanted electrodes in epilepsy patients. Tang and colleagues reconstructed aspects of meaning from brain scans. Kunz and colleagues decoded instructed imagined sentences.
missing: Detailed recovery of unfamiliar events must preserve people, places, sequence and sensory details while distinguishing similar memories.
Specified events must be installed and later recalled, with controls for suggestion, conditioning and learned reporting.
Experiments must connect particular memory content to molecular changes, connections between brain cells and activity across brain regions.

milestones.label: Unfamiliar memories are recovered with faithful detail
milestones.explanation: Readout would have to match recollection for events excluded from training, including unpredictable details, and outperform story-based guessing. Independent event records would help identify errors in recollection.

milestones.label: Installed events return through ordinary memory cues
milestones.explanation: Animal tests would first have to show natural-cue recall of specified, unexperienced events, with controls for conditioning and suggestion. This would establish a basis for later studies in consenting humans.

milestones.label: Selective changes reveal how a particular memory is stored
milestones.explanation: Experiments would have to alter molecular features or connections between brain cells needed for a particular event while preserving comparison memories and general abilities. This would connect memory manipulation to storage.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and establish practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to replicate results across people and events, measuring errors, durability, training needs, invasive access and unintended changes. This would establish reliability and conditions for stopping readout.

uncertain: The brain signals predicting recalled concepts may reflect general meaning or context shared across experiences.
Acceptable error rates, required durability and sufficient animal evidence remain to be defined.
Restoring an original memory depends on access to its original content or a surviving trace.

page.title: Neural decoding and implantation of human episodic memories
page.definition: A remembered personal event can be reconstructed from brain activity, including its people, place, event order and sensory details. Neural intervention can also introduce a specified, unexperienced event subsequently retrieved as an episodic memory: a recollection situated in space and time.

goal.need: In 10 people, brain activity distinguished three learned film memories. In 14 epilepsy patients, content-targeted hippocampal stimulation changed recognition performance in 22.4% of patient–category combinations, with both improvements and impairments. These results motivate separate tests of which episodic details can be recovered and which can be introduced by neural intervention.

statements.body: Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, Restoring Active Memory programme
statements.quote: technology that can effectively bridge the gaps that interfere with an individual’s ability to encode new memories or retrieve old ones.
statements.context: DARPA described the intended function of implantable memory neuroprosthetics on 9 July 2014. This is a memory-restoration goal.

statements.body: NIH BRAIN-funded UCLA–University of Iowa research team
statements.quote: to decode and modulate selective memories before, during, and after sleep.
statements.context: The project page identifies NIH BRAIN support and a performance period of September 2021 through August 2026.

statements.body: Hospital for Sick Children-led artificial-memory research team
statements.quote: artificially implant a memory for an otherwise never experienced event.
statements.context: Vetere and colleagues state this objective in a study of artificial associative memories in mice.

completion.title: Independent experiments confirm both neural decoding and implantation of specified human episodes.
completion.criterion: Peer-reviewed demonstrations establish both operations in consenting humans, and independent researchers confirm each using newly collected data. Readout recovers an episode's prespecified people, place, event order and sensory details from recall activity, matching separately elicited recollection. Write-in introduces a specified episode without experiencing or being told it; after intervention ceases, natural cues elicit its details in recollection and behavior. Blinded comparisons distinguish the intended episode from similar episodes, suggestion and trained responses. The readout test withholds target-episode content from decoder training and inference.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; fallback operational definition after the searches described in basis.
completion.basis: Searches covered DARPA RAM, NIH BRAIN roadmaps and funded projects, engram criteria, ClinicalTrials.gov, ISO/FDA terminology and memory-decoding prizes. No published test combining detailed human episodic readout and specified episodic implantation was found. This Atlas fallback combines the two capabilities. Independent confirmation follows the National Academies' rationale for repeating research.

milestones.title: Brain activity identifies which of three learned episodes a person recalls above 1/3 chance.
milestones.criterion: Identify which of three learned film events a person recalls from hippocampal functional magnetic resonance imaging, with decoding significantly above the task's chance level of 0.33. Chadwick and colleagues reported this result in 10 participants on 11 March 2010. Decoding also exceeded chance in entorhinal and parahippocampal regions. The output identifies an episode from a known set.
milestones.set_by: Chadwick and colleagues, published three-film experimental protocol and Figure 2 caption in Current Biology; this is a study-specific test.
milestones.threshold_quote: the dashed line at 0.33 represents chance-level performance.

milestones.title: Reactivating learning-tagged neurons evokes a rodent memory's behavioral expression without its cue.
milestones.criterion: Activate neurons tagged during learning and elicit memory-specific behavior without the natural retrieval cue. In Liu and colleagues' study, published on 22 March 2012, 12 mice showed increased freezing in a different context during light activation of tagged hippocampal neurons (p < 0.001). No-shock and fluorescent-protein control groups contained 12 mice each and showed no increased light-induced freezing.
milestones.set_by: The gain-of-function criterion used in engram research, stated by Josselyn and Tonegawa in Science in 2020; formulated primarily for rodent memory experiments.
milestones.threshold_quote: artificially activating engram cells induces memory retrieval, in the absence of any natural sensory retrieval cues.

milestones.title: A memory formed entirely by brain stimulation guides behavior to its real sensory cue.
milestones.criterion: The learning event occurs entirely through brain intervention. A real external sensory cue subsequently evokes behavior specific to the intended association and its positive or negative value. On 29 April 2019, Vetere and colleagues reported odor avoidance 24 hours after entirely intracranial associative training: 12 mice received paired stimulation and 8 received unpaired stimulation; odor preference differed between groups (p = 0.016). This demonstrates an artificial odor–aversion association.
milestones.set_by: Artificial-memory implantation criteria stated by Vetere and colleagues in Nature Neuroscience and reiterated by Josselyn and Tonegawa; applied here to the mouse associative-memory experiment.
milestones.threshold_quote: the ‘learning event’ should take place entirely intracranially

milestones.title: A neural decoder recovers the prespecified details of a human episode withheld from training.
milestones.criterion: Recover the prespecified people, place, event order and sensory details of a human episode from neural activity during recall, concordant with separately elicited recollection. Target-episode content is withheld from decoder training and inference. Blinded comparisons with similar episodes and predictions made without neural recordings establish that the recovered details depend on episode-specific neural information. No demonstration meeting this definition was identified.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; searches of episodic-decoding studies, NIH BRAIN project goals, standards and trial records found no external acceptance criterion for detailed reconstruction.

milestones.title: Neural intervention installs a specified human episode later recalled through natural cues.
milestones.criterion: Introduce a specified episode by neural intervention without the subject experiencing or being told that episode. After intervention ceases, natural cues elicit its prespecified people, place, event order and sensory details in recollection and behavior. Controls distinguish retrieval of the intended episode from suggestion, conditioning alone and trained reporting. No human demonstration meeting this definition was identified. Independent confirmation of both this result and m4 remains necessary for completion.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; searches of artificial-memory criteria, human memory-prosthesis studies, DARPA RAM and trial records found no external human episodic-implantation acceptance criterion.

not_found: No external numerical fidelity, error-rate or retention threshold was found for detailed human episodic reconstruction or implantation.

results.finding: In 15 participants, recalled concepts were decoded above chance before sleep (p = 1.03 × 10−4).
results.detail: Models were trained on neural activity and concept labels from viewing the target episode. They predicted mentions of selected concepts, not the full people, place, event order and sensory details. The authors could not establish that the decoded signal represented an episode-specific memory trace.
results.quote:
Concept decoding compared to chance (50%) shows significant effects for both
conditions (presleep: p = 1.03 × 10−4, postsleep: p = 4.52 × 10−5; Wilcoxon signed-rank), indicating
consistent decoding of concepts across participants.

results.finding: For 2 subjects imagining five stories, decoder predictions identified the correct story in 100% of scans.
results.detail: The study decoded imagined narratives, but the supplied text does not establish recall of personal episodes or recovery of their prespecified details.
results.quote: For each scan, the decoder prediction was most similar to the reference transcript of the correct story (100% identification accuracy).

results.finding: In 12 fear-conditioned mice, light activation of learning-tagged hippocampal neurons increased freezing in a different context (p < 0.001).
results.detail: Neither the no-shock nor the fluorescent-protein control group showed increased light-induced freezing; each contained 12 mice.
results.quote: In contrast, after fear conditioning, freezing levels during light-on epochs were significantly higher compared with light-off epochs, which indicated light-induced fear memory recall

results.finding: In 11 mice, activating learning-tagged dentate gyrus neurons increased freezing versus controls (p = 0.0002).
results.detail: The experiment used chemogenetic activation in a neutral context, with 11 mice per group. It was not the specified 2012 Liu study and does not report its 12-mouse no-shock and fluorescent-protein control groups.
results.quote: Activating DG engram cells using CNO resulted in increased freezing behavior compared to mCherry control mice

results.finding: In 50 participants, feature ratings for 12 of 20 autobiographical scenarios were reconstructed significantly above chance.
results.detail: A decoder trained on sentence-reading data reconstructed broad experiential feature ratings, not the specified people, place, event order and sensory details of an episode. Participants were cued with generic scenario prompts.
results.quote: 12 out of 20 scenarios were reconstructed with statistically significant accuracies.

results.finding: In 10 participants, hippocampal fMRI identified recalled film episodes significantly above the 0.33 chance level.
results.detail: Decoding also exceeded chance in the entorhinal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus.
results.quote: Proportion accuracy values are shown on the vertical axis; the dashed line at 0.33 represents chance-level performance. All three areas were significantly above chance-level performance, with hippocampus (HC) accuracy significantly greater than both entorhinal cortex (EC) and parahippocampal gyrus (PHG)

results.finding: In 10 participants, fMRI decoding distinguished recalled episodes from a set of 3 learned films.
results.detail: The classifier identified an episode from a known set and was trained on data from those memories. It did not recover the prespecified details of an episode withheld from training and inference.
results.quote: This analysis revealed episodic memory decoding in the hippocampus for every participant, showing that it is possible to predict which specific episodic memory was being recalled solely from the pattern of fMRI BOLD signals across voxels in the hippocampus.

results.finding: In 50 participants, recalled autobiographical scenario pairs were discriminated with a mean accuracy of 64%.
results.detail: The study used two-alternative discrimination of autobiographical scenarios from cortical fMRI, rather than identifying one of three learned film events from hippocampal fMRI.
results.quote:
Scenario pairs were discriminated with a mean accuracy of 64%, with significant permutation tests (
p
< 0.05) in 25/50 of participants.

results.finding: In 10 participants, hippocampal fMRI distinguished recall of three viewed film episodes.
results.detail: The classifier identified which familiar episode was recalled; it did not reconstruct its people, place, event order and sensory details. Training included data from the target memories.
results.quote: This analysis revealed episodic memory decoding in the hippocampus for every participant, showing that it is possible to predict which specific episodic memory was being recalled solely from the pattern of fMRI BOLD signals across voxels in the hippocampus.

results.finding: In 15 participants, hippocampal fMRI decoded recalled film memories significantly above chance (P = 0.04).
results.detail: The study classified four overlapping film memories, with a chance level of 0.25, rather than the criterion's three memories and chance level of 0.33. Decoding was not significant in the neighboring regions tested.
results.quote: In both analyses, only the HC results are significantly above chance.

results.finding: In 20 mice, odor preference differed between paired and unpaired intracranial training groups (p = 0.016).
results.detail: Twelve mice received paired stimulation and eight received unpaired stimulation. The paired group avoided the corresponding real odor 24 hours later.
results.quote: In this test, mice avoided the acetophenone (M72-activating odorant) side of the apparatus.
